Chapter 2: The Weight of Tradition—Marriage, Womanhood, and the Loss of Innocence
Growing up in a world where tradition is both a comfort and a cage... that transition from girlhood to womanhood often sneaks up when you’re least expecting it, and honestly? You’re rarely ready for it. Those first signs—your first period, the quiet advice whispered by older women, suddenly being told to cover up—these all hint that life’s about to shift in a big way.
But the reasons for it all? They stay hidden, wrapped up in secrecy. Your body suddenly feels like a battleground—something to be proud of, but also a source of shame. Your mind races, trying to catch up with all these new rules that seem to appear overnight.
And then, there’s marriage. It isn’t really a choice; it’s more like a destination that’s already picked out for you. Families, hoping to secure your future and their own place in the community, arrange a match with a man you barely know. The wedding day itself? It’s a whirlwind of colors, music, and faces—a celebration where you’re both the star and somehow invisible at the same time. Your own hopes and dreams get swept away in the noise of tradition.
Those first days in your new life… they’re filled with confusion and fear. The house feels strange, your husband distant and unpredictable. You know what’s expected: obedience, submission, and the hope that you’ll bear children. But reality is so much messier. Intimacy, which is supposed to bring you closer, can feel forced or even painful. You find yourself longing for the safety of your childhood—the comfort of your mother’s arms.
Most people think marriage brings security. But for so many women, it’s actually the start of a new kind of loneliness. Husbands, wrapped up in their own worries, don’t offer much comfort or understanding. So you end up navigating your new life alone, your needs quietly pushed aside. The house fills up with unspoken tensions, and the constant threat of someone’s disapproval lingers in the air.
In all this, you learn to hide who you really are. You become an expert at playing the role everyone expects, even as you feel yourself slipping away. The daily routines—cooking, cleaning, serving—turn into a kind of armor, shielding you from the sting of rejection. Still, underneath it all, there’s a longing that never quite disappears—the hope for connection, for love, for freedom.
And then comes motherhood. The birth of children brings joy, but also new burdens. Sure, being a mom is celebrated, but it comes with its own pile of expectations and sacrifices. You pour yourself into caring for your children, finding little moments of happiness in their laughter and innocence. But the demands of family life? They leave almost no space for your own dreams. The world outside your home starts to feel far away—a place you can only visit in your imagination.
Over time, the distance between who you are and who you’re supposed to be just keeps growing. Loneliness settles in, a constant reminder of what tradition can cost. Many women, facing the same struggle, learn to accept their fate, finding small comforts wherever they can. But for some, the desire for something more—something real—never fades away.
The truth is, losing your innocence isn’t a single moment. It’s a slow unraveling. The girl who once dreamed of love and adventure becomes a woman who measures her days in chores and compromises. And yet, even in the darkest times, there’s always a spark of hope—a belief that life can change, that happiness might still be possible.
